column3: Near-verbatim parallel: factions differ and the wrongdoers face woe from a painful Day.
Links disagreement to God's judgment on the Day of Resurrection, though over Sabbath observance.
Mary's slander supplies a concrete later example of the false claims surrounding her and Jesus.
Directly parallels the woe for disbelievers from their promised Day.
Immediately identifies Jesus as Mary's son and the truth disputed by the factions.
Addresses disbelief in God's signs, a central element of the focus warning, without its dispute setting.
Shares a warning of punishment on a great Day but concerns the she-camel.
The next ayah continues the warning with the Day when people come to God.
God's final judgment over matters people dispute directly illuminates the factions' disagreement.
Condemns division and disagreement after clear proofs, followed by a warning of great punishment.
The preceding denial that God takes a son states the truth at issue in the factions' dispute.
The greatness of Abraham's ransom does not clarify disagreement, disbelief, or the Day.
Uses factions as hostile confederates, offering only a limited comparison to the divided parties.
The following warning of the Day of Regret develops the focus ayah's painful-Day threat.
Shu'ayb's ethical distinction from his people is unrelated to the disputed claim about Jesus.
Its great Day reinforces the eschatological gravity but lacks dispute or disbelief context.
In the parallel Jesus discourse, Satan's obstruction precedes the factions' disagreement and warning.
A general condemnation of human disbelief offers limited support for the focus warning.
Pairs woe with disbelief and punishment, though its subject is denial of purposeful creation.
Jesus' call to worship God alone immediately precedes and explains the ensuing factional disagreement.
A great announcement alone is too general to illuminate the focus ayah.
References a day of hostile factions but in a historical warning rather than a doctrinal dispute.
Within the same surah, Abraham warns of punishment for rejecting God, echoing the focus warning.
Names a matter over which people disagree, but it concerns the great announcement rather than Jesus.
A prophet's warning of punishment on a great Day parallels the focus's warning form.
God's party contrasts with hostile factions only at the broad theme of affiliation.
Explicitly states that God will decide on the Day of Resurrection what people disputed.
The formula of woe is shared, but its target is heedless worshippers rather than disbelieving factions.
Jesus as a sign and a decreed matter provides the immediate narrative basis for later disputes over him.
A disbelievers' difficult Day echoes the threat but lacks the focus's factional disagreement.
Warns those who fabricate claims as divine revelation, relevant to false theological claims about Jesus.
Zechariah's concern for his heirs has no material link to the focus ayah.
Its mention of disbelievers is unrelated to Jesus, disagreement, or the final warning.
Lists former hostile factions, a distant lexical and historical parallel only.
States that people continue to differ, providing a general frame for the factions' disagreement.
The Quran clarifies matters over which a religious community differs, paralleling the focus's disputed truth.
A messenger's monotheistic warning of a great Day resembles the focus warning in form and purpose.
Mary's return with Jesus begins the immediate sequence of accusations underlying the later dispute.
Upholding testimony does not materially illuminate the factions or their punishment.
Associates denial of clear truth by factions with the Fire, closely paralleling the focus warning.
The reminder of human creation does not clarify this dispute or its stated punishment.
Describes people as holding contradictory speech, a general analogue to factional disagreement.
A revealed book becomes disputed, with final decision deferred by God, closely matching the focus pattern.
Doubt about meeting God relates loosely to the coming Day but not to the factions' dispute.
General disbelief and hostile rushing toward the messenger offer only a distant comparison.
Directly parallels disagreement over revelation and God's deferred judgment between disputants.
The accusation against Mary's family is an immediate source of the contested claims about Jesus.
God's universal witness is too general to illuminate the focus ayah.
Disbelievers face a Day with witnesses and no excuse, supporting the focus's eschatological warning.
Mary's gesture toward the infant directly advances the narrative that the factions later contest.
Punishment for disbelief is relevant only generally; the ritual critique is otherwise unrelated.
Witness and witnessed do not bear on the disputed doctrine or stated warning.
Jesus' infant declaration immediately supplies the truth against which later factions differ.
General persistent disbelief explains the warned group only at a broad level.
Contrasts unbelievers with the God-fearing on the Day of Resurrection, supporting the judgment theme.
The surah's later separation of rebellious sects develops the theme of divided groups under judgment.
Return to the Knower of the unseen and seen loosely supports final accountability.
Addresses Jesus, disbelievers, and God's final judgment over what people differed about.
A monotheistic warning of painful-Day punishment closely echoes the focus's warning language.
God's testimony to divine unity is broadly relevant to the truth disputed about Jesus.
Depicts the final judgment with prophets and witnesses, grounding the focus's promised painful Day.
Jesus' continuing speech in the immediate narrative establishes his prophetic and devotional identity.
Deliverance from Noah's great distress does not clarify the focus ayah.
Lists religious groups and says God will decide between them on the Day of Resurrection.
Mary's earlier consolation is part of the local narrative but does not directly bear on the dispute.
General disbelief and obstruction of God's way only loosely relate to the warned disbelievers.
A people who reject their messenger receive punishment on a great Day, echoing the warning structure.
Being turned away from truth is a distant conceptual link to disbelief.
Disbelief in God and His messenger is relevant only generally to the focus's disbelievers.
Opposition from disbelievers is broadly relevant but not to factional disagreement or the Day.
Jesus' immediate self-description continues the corrective account contested by the factions.
Directly assigns every dispute to God's judgment, clarifying the resolution of the factions' difference.
Promises Hell to those who disbelieve in their Lord, reinforcing the focus's punishment warning.
The surah's later identification of those most deserving of Hell only loosely develops the warning.
Rejecting a received reminder offers a general analogy to the focus's disbelievers.
Military confederates are only a lexical parallel to the theological factions in the focus ayah.
The unseen alone has no material relation to the focus ayah.
The presence of sons does not illuminate disagreement, disbelief, or punishment.
Woe on that Day for deniers closely supports the focus's warning formula.
Jesus' birth, death, and resurrection framing in the immediate passage relates to the disputed identity.
Revelation, testimony, and disbelief in divine judgment broadly illuminate disputes over sacred truth.
Near-exact parallel: God judges on the Day of Resurrection what people differed about.
Mary's withdrawal while bearing Jesus is part of the immediate narrative background to the dispute.
Lying about God and rejecting truth lead to Hell, relevant to the focus's censured disbelievers.
Explicitly joins disagreement after knowledge with God's judgment on the Day of Resurrection.
Return to God in the local surah supports ultimate accountability but not the specific dispute.
The Day and God's knowledge of seen and unseen provide only a broad eschatological connection.
Reward for obedient believers after injury does not illuminate the focus ayah.
Mary's labor is local narrative background but has no direct connection to the factions' claim.
Disbelievers call a messenger's warning strange, a limited parallel to rejecting truth about Jesus.
The question of a deferred day alone does not add relevance to the focus ayah.
Disbelief that also turns others from God's way resembles the harmful stance of the warned group.
The Day when secrets are tested offers a general connection to final exposure and judgment.
The command not to obey disbelievers is broadly relevant but lacks the focus's central themes.
A multitude from the earlier generations has no material connection to the focus ayah.
Disbelievers are told to enter Hell that Day, reinforcing the focus's punitive warning.
A small number from later generations has no material connection to the focus ayah.
God's witness between opponents and the loss of those who disbelieve in Him broadly fit the dispute.
Rules of visiting the Prophet's household do not clarify the focus ayah.
Disbelievers receiving recompense supports accountability only in a general sense.
Directly rejects the claim that God has taken a son, the core error behind the disputed truth about Jesus.
States that the People of the Book differed only after knowledge came to them, closely framing culpable religious division.
Identifies Jesus as the Messiah and a word from God, supplying the revealed description contested by later factions.
Jesus calls people to worship God alone, a direct parallel to 19:36 and the truth over which they differ.
Compares Jesus before God to Adam, directly correcting exaggerated claims about his exceptional birth.
Affirms the revealed account as truth and forbids doubt, directly relevant to the disputed matter.
Provides a formal response to continuing dispute over Jesus after knowledge has come.
Records conflicting false claims concerning Jesus, making it a direct example of dispute over his person and fate.
Connects belief concerning Jesus with the Day of Resurrection, when he will be a witness against the People of the Book.
Forbids excess in religion, defines Jesus as God's messenger, and rejects saying Three.
Rejects the idea that the Messiah is above being God's servant, supporting the focus passage's corrective account.
Explicitly calls disbelief the claim that God is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary.
Assigns final judgment to God over the matters in which communities differ.
Explicitly condemns deifying the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, and warns of exclusion from Paradise.
Condemns the claim that God is one of three, a central factional error concerning Jesus.
Stresses that the Messiah and his mother ate food, directly correcting claims of their divinity.
Depicts God's questioning of Jesus about whether he told people to take him and his mother as gods.
Condemns those who split their religion and became factions, directly echoing the focus ayah's parties.
Rejects attributing sons and daughters to God without knowledge, directly addressing the underlying theological error.
Rejects God's having a child by affirming His unique creative sovereignty.
Names the Christian claim that the Messiah is God's son and likens it to earlier disbelief.
Condemns taking religious authorities and the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, as lords besides God.
Rejects the assertion that God has taken a child and condemns speaking without knowledge.
Describes the Hereafter as a day gathered and witnessed, helping explain the focus ayah's solemn Day imagery.
Rejects attributing offspring to God, a broader parallel to the error at issue in claims about Jesus.
Affirms that God has not taken a child, directly opposing the doctrinal claim under dispute.
Warns those who say that God has taken a child.
Condemns the unsupported claim that God has taken a child as a grave false statement.
Records the claim that the Most Merciful has taken a child, directly extending the same doctrinal polemic.
Restates the attribution of a child to the Most Merciful, identifying the offense behind the factions' error.
States that taking a child is unfitting for the Most Merciful.
Affirms that everyone in the heavens and earth comes to the Most Merciful only as a servant, including Jesus.
Rejects the claim that God has taken children and calls those alleged children honored servants.
Denies that God has taken a child or has any other god, refuting the theological excess at issue.
Affirms God's sole sovereignty and denies that He has taken a child.
Commands turning to God and forbids joining those who divided their religion.
Describes religious division into factions, each party rejoicing in its own position.
States that God has not taken a child and affirms His absolute oneness and mastery.
Reports that people divided the one religion God prescribed, providing the wider pattern of religious factionalism.
States that they did not divide until knowledge came, and that God will judge between them.
Condemns treating part of God's servants as a share of Him, a theological error developed in the parallel Jesus passage.
Shows people raising an argumentative clamor when the son of Mary is presented as an example.
Records the disputants' argument about Jesus and identifies it as contentious disputation.
Defines Jesus as a servant whom God favored and made an example for Israel.
Connects Jesus with knowledge of the Hour and commands that it not be doubted.
Jesus comes with clear proofs and says he will clarify some of what people differ about.
Jesus calls to worship God alone, immediately preceding the parallel account of factions differing.
Affirms that God's majesty precludes taking a wife or child.
Concise categorical denial that God begets or is begotten, directly refuting sonship claims.
